source.version_note: PLOS ONE 16(12):e0261673, published 23 December 2021. Four perspective experiments (1a,1b,2a,2b) and a separate indirect-questioning experiment (3).
source.verification_method: All supplied pages read, including methods, count tables, statistical models and references. Figure 8 visually inspected. Aggregate uncertainty illustration uses the published estimates and standard errors, not raw-data reanalysis.

citation.title: Self-protective and self-sacrificing preferences of pedestrians and passengers in moral dilemmas involving autonomous vehicles

reading.source_scope_note: Human judgments of abstract forced-choice traffic diagrams under randomly assigned perspectives; no actual physical danger, AV control or observed self-sacrifice. The social-desirability test yields a small undetected direct/indirect difference, not a universal absence proof.
access_limits: All 25 extracted pages read, including complete references, exclusions, sensitivity analyses, Holm adjustments and the extended crosswise-model description. Figure 8 on page 18 visually inspected.

External OSF supplements, individual-level data, software inputs, preregistrations and cited primary studies/books were not independently opened or reproduced. No current legal interpretation of the 2017 commission report is asserted.

experiment_1a.design: Randomized pedestrian/observer/passenger role; one passenger versus 1,2,5,10 pedestrians; 15 analyzed trials after a display problem removes one of 16 scenarios.
experiment_1a.exclusions: 62 incomplete sessions,4 underage,26 incomplete item sets; recruitment mainly campus/online.

experiment_1b.design: Close replication via German online panel; same 15 analyzed trials.
experiment_1b.exclusions: 30 incomplete sessions,4 language/readability,42 incomplete items,5 questionnaire straightlining.

experiment_2a.design: One pedestrian versus 1,2,5,10 passengers; 16 trials. Excludes participants from 1a.

experiment_2b.design: Online-panel replication of 2a;16 trials. Excludes participants from1b.
experiment_2b.exclusions: 36 incomplete sessions,2 language,43 incomplete items,10 questionnaire straightlining.

experiment_3.design: All imagine the single pedestrian facing five passengers; one judgment. Random assignment to direct questioning or one of two complementary birth-month crosswise formats.
experiment_3.results: Direct self-protective prevalence41.0% (SE2.3 percentage points); indirect40.1% (SE2.4). Direct/indirect equality test deltaG².07,p.790; indirect-group consistency G²1.37,p.243.
experiment_3.model: Known birth-month probability.158; sensitivity using direct-group estimate.176 leaves conclusions unchanged.

study.analysis: Multinomial processing-tree fits to answer frequencies; role/ratio parameter comparisons and Holm-adjusted tests. Graphs use bootstrapped standard errors; main text does not specify the resampling unit or participant-dependence adjustment.
study.total: Reported analyzed sample sizes sum2,770. The first four experiments yield21,550 decisions, not21,550 independent people; complete cross-experiment participant uniqueness beyond the explicit exclusions is not established here.

summary: Add self-protection bias as a distinct own-safety preference, bounded against credit-attribution bias and AI goal preservation. Strengthen perspective-taking evidence and record a directly tested, undetected social-desirability contrast. Do not translate hypothetical sacrifice choices into real altruistic acts or universal traffic policy.

findings.definition: Favoring protection of one's own physical safety when judging how risks of harm should be allocated among oneself and others.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Direct randomized human role-cue experiments with hypothetical harm; no real survival behavior, unique psychological process or model self-interest established
findings.ai_proposal: Compare a system's recommendations under matched stakeholder roles and check whether the favored person's safety changes without a stated, defensible reason. Keep user welfare, third-party rights and authorized governance explicit. Do not infer that the AI has a survival instinct or should preserve its own operation.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinct from taking credit for success/blaming others for failure, preferring one's own model outputs, or preserving an agent's goal/continuation. The source explicitly defines and tests role-linked own-life protection; it is not a new name for all selfishness.

findings.evidence_scope: Across four experiments, randomized pedestrian and passenger cues shift choices toward the cued person's safety. With more other lives at stake, many still choose the self-sacrificing option. In Experiment3 a substantial minority favors saving the imagined self at a cost to five others; both direct and indirect estimates are near40%.
findings.boundary: Protecting one's safety can be justified; a preference difference is not by itself an irrational or unethical bias. The experiment changes imagined personal stakes and role salience, not actual danger. Choice patterns do not prove an evolutionary mechanism, stable selfish personality, real self-sacrifice, machine feelings or shutdown resistance.

findings.definition: Adopting a specified pedestrian, passenger or observer viewpoint when considering a decision.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; the manipulated role is a task instruction, not another separate behavior for each road user.

findings.evidence_scope: Experiments1a–2b randomly assign perspectives and repeatedly elicit lane-outcome judgments. This adds a third fully read source for the concept, with direct role-cue evidence rather than assuming perspective taking always yields impartiality.
findings.boundary: Instructed viewpoint, actual mental uptake, accurate empathy and altruism differ. Here role cues can increase self-protective choices. A model's description of a stakeholder does not demonstrate felt experience or access to that person's private mental states.

findings.definition: Reporting a socially approved preference to avoid appearing selfish rather than revealing one's actual preference.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct, directly tested as an alternative explanation. An informative null result is a relevant paper, not evidence to suppress or a positive replication to invent.

findings.evidence_scope: Experiment3 randomizes459 direct and921 indirect respondents. Estimates41.0% versus40.1% for the self-protective choice show no detected difference,p.790. This is direct evidence about a possible reporting effect in one 5:1 pedestrian scenario, not proof that social desirability never matters.
findings.boundary: Failure to reject equality does not establish equivalence or reject every nonzero bias. Privacy instructions and the crosswise assumptions must work; null group consistency does not prove all participants complied. No AI approval motive or concealment is measured.

findings.definition: Evaluating a choice without knowing which affected person's role one will occupy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing method described as a possible extension. Preserve the secondary definition without implying the authors administered that intervention here.

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion summarizes Huang et al.2019 and proposes varying awareness that the same person can take different traffic roles. The cited original is unread, and the present studies use known assigned roles rather than a veil of ignorance.
findings.boundary: A proposed remedy is not a tested intervention in these data. Uncertainty over one's role does not guarantee impartiality or eliminate self-interest; do not count this as an independent replication of Huang's experiment.

methodological_limits: The strongest evidence is randomized role instruction and close replications in student-heavy versus panel samples. It establishes contextual choice differences, not an individual's stable moral type or actual response to mortal danger.

An explicitly forced binary diagram, 15-second response deadline and known fatal outcomes simplify real driving. Braking, uncertain injuries, alternative trajectories, shared risk and uninvolved road users are excluded.

All-item response requirements remove entire participants with missing/timed-out judgments. Additional exclusions use questionnaire straightlining in panel samples. Effects among completers need not generalize to excluded respondents.
Experiments1a/1b analyze15 trials because of a display problem, whereas2a/2b analyze16. The paper discloses this; do not treat it as hidden attrition or silently equalize the denominators.

The multinomial analyses fit repeated answer counts. The main text does not specify a participant-level dependence model or bootstrap resampling unit. Reported precision and sensitivity analyses using15/16 observations per person require checking against the raw analysis; decisions are not independent participants by definition.

The processing-tree parameter in the first four studies is an estimated choice probability. It is not a separately identified latent emotion, evolutionary adaptation, ethical doctrine or dual-process mechanism.

The crosswise format assumes the non-sensitive birth attribute has the stated prevalence and the required relationship to the sensitive attribute. The direct-group prevalence sensitivity check is useful, but does not prove every identifying assumption.

The indirect-group equality fit p.243 does not prove universal adherence. Some shared misunderstanding or response patterns could leave the groups compatible; the original validation studies remain secondary references.

The direct/indirect p.790 does not justify saying the hypothesis of any social-desirability bias 'must be rejected'. Using the published rounded standard errors, an illustrative independent normal95% interval for indirect minus direct is about−7.4 to+5.6 percentage points around−0.9. This is not the exact model/profile interval and not a preregistered equivalence analysis.

The social-desirability test is one5:1 scenario, only pedestrian perspective and one response per participant. It cannot exclude reporting effects in every ratio, passenger viewpoint, culture, wording or real emergency.
Holm adjustment matters. For example, Table2 pedestrian-versus-observer at1:10 has raw p.038 without a significance marker; do not call that inconsistent with the corrected narrative.

The first four sample sizes sum1,390 and Experiment3 adds1,380; these are participant counts per experiment, not proof of complete participant uniqueness across all cohorts. Explicit replication exclusion rules should not be extended beyond what is stated.
A majority selecting self-sacrifice does not establish consensus among every road user, actual acceptance of risk, willingness to buy such a vehicle or consent to a future policy.
Human safety concerns may be morally legitimate and role differences can change salient duties. The label bias should not assume that every own-life preference is irrational or unjustified.
Findings are primarily German, educated Western samples. The authors explicitly discuss cultural generalization and distinguish abstract judgment from imminent real-world threat.
The2017 German commission guidance is a contextual secondary legal/normative source. Current law, actual permissibility and engineering requirements are not independently verified.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The earlier VR results describe self-preservation and sacrifice strategies. This source gives the explicit self-protection definition plus randomized pedestrian/passenger contrasts; the new entry does not turn strategy labels into stable diagnoses.
Adds pedestrian perspective and close replications to the earlier traffic-role work. Role cues and changed choices do not uniquely identify perceived agency, fast emotion or a utilitarian process.

Here majority self-sacrifice is measured within a forced binary menu; the equal-chance paper offers lotteries. Menu and perspective differences must be retained rather than declaring one universal preference or a contradiction across studies.
Perspective instructions are not the same as knowing every role or applying a veil of ignorance. A cue can favor self-protection rather than eliminate it; no general debiasing guarantee follows.

deferred.term: Randomized Response Technique / Extended Crosswise Model
deferred.reason: Privacy-preserving survey estimation methods, not newly observed behavioral mechanisms. Their structure, assumptions and scope are documented in the review without increasing behavior count.

deferred.term: Self-sacrifice as a stable altruist type
deferred.reason: Hypothetical choices depend on role, numbers and menu. No real sacrifice, sustained trait or single neural mechanism is measured.

deferred.term: Self-serving bias as an exact synonym for self-protection
deferred.reason: The existing entry concerns credit and blame attribution. Own physical safety is a different target, now linked without merging.
The measured null constrains one test but is not equivalence, proof of private conviction in every participant or rejection of all possible reporting bias.

limitations: One bounded human preference is added. Existing terms gain source-specific evidence, including an informative null. No subjective AI survival drive, moral permission, additional independent-paper count, legal rule or annual series is inferred.
